Tokens & Embeddings

How text becomes the numbers a model can think with

A language model never sees letters. It sees a list of integers, one per token, and the first thing it does with each integer is look up a vector: a few hundred numbers that stand for what the token means. This chapter builds both halves from real text. You will train a byte-pair tokeniser on Pride and Prejudice, and squeeze 17 million words of Wikipedia into 100-dimensional word vectors where meaning becomes distance and direction. The map holds all 6,000 of those words. Type a word, or click anywhere on the map: the lines join it to its nearest neighbours.

Tokens
The pieces a model reads; GPT-2 has 50,257 of them
Embeddings
One learned vector per token, looked up from a table
The idea
Words that keep the same company end up close together
The problem

Text is not numbers, yet

A neural network multiplies and adds. Before it can read a sentence, something has to cut the sentence into pieces from a fixed list, the vocabulary, and replace each piece by its position in that list. That something is the tokeniser. The obvious choices both fail. Whole words give short sequences but an endless vocabulary, and any word the tokeniser never met becomes a useless [UNK]. Single characters or bytes never meet an unknown, but turn every sentence into a long, slow string of tiny pieces. Modern models use subwords: common words whole, rare ones in a few pieces. Type anything, including a name, a typo or an emoji, and switch between the four schemes.

\[ \begin{gathered} \text{text} \;\xrightarrow{\ \ \tau\ \ }\; (t_1, t_2, \dots, t_n) \\ t_i \in \{0, 1, \dots, |V|-1\} \end{gathered} \]
Read it as: the tokeniser τ turns a string into a sequence of n integers, each the index of a piece in the vocabulary V. Two numbers matter: n, because a model's cost grows with the length of what it reads, and |V|, because the model needs a vector, and an output score, for every entry. Every scheme trades one against the other.
Say it“Tau maps the text to a sequence t-one to t-n, each an integer from zero to the vocabulary size minus one.”
tokens n
vocabulary |V|
unknown or fallback tokens
characters per token

The algorithm

Byte-pair encoding, by hand

Byte-pair encoding began in 1994 as a compression trick (Gage) and became a tokeniser in 2016 (Sennrich, Haddow & Birch). The rule is almost embarrassingly simple. Start with every word spelt out in single characters, with _ marking where a word ends. Count every pair of neighbouring symbols, weighted by how often each word occurs. Glue the most frequent pair into one new symbol, and repeat. Each merge adds one entry to the vocabulary; the list of merges, in order, is the tokeniser. Below is Sennrich’s own toy corpus. Press Merge and watch the pieces grow, or type your own words (word:count).

\[ (a^\star, b^\star) = \arg\max_{(a,\,b)} \; \sum_{w} f(w)\; n_{ab}(w) \]
Read it as: f(w) is how often word w occurs in the corpus; nab(w) is how many times symbol a is directly followed by symbol b in w’s current spelling. Pick the pair with the largest weighted count (ties go to the alphabetically first pair), replace every adjacent “a b” by the new symbol “ab”, and count again.
Say it“The pair to merge is the a, b that maximises the sum over words of the word’s frequency times how often a is followed by b in it.”
merges so far
vocabulary size
tokens in the corpus

Real text

How many merges?

Now the same algorithm on the first 50 chapters of Pride and Prejudice: 117,661 words and punctuation marks, 6,154 different ones, written in 76 different characters. Its first merges glue word endings: e_, d_, t_, then th. After a few hundred, whole common words appear; after a few thousand, nearly every word Austen uses often is a single token, while rare and unseen words still break into familiar pieces. The number of merges is a dial between a small vocabulary and short sequences. Turn it and watch three sentences from the last 11 chapters, which the tokeniser never saw.

\[ \begin{aligned} |V| &= |A| + M \\ \text{tokens per word} &= \frac{\#\,\text{tokens}}{\#\,\text{words}} \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: A is the starting alphabet (here 76 characters plus the end-of-word mark _, so |A| = 77), and every one of the M merges adds exactly one symbol. Tokens per word (sometimes called fertility) measures how finely the text is chopped: 1 means every word is a single token. Measured on held-out chapters, it tells you what the tokeniser will do to text it has never seen.
Say it“The vocabulary size is the alphabet size plus the number of merges; tokens per word is tokens divided by words.”
vocabulary |V|
held-out tokens per word

tokens in the sentence

From ids to vectors

The embedding table

A token id is a name, not a quantity: token 902 is not “more” than token 186. The honest way to feed it to a network is a one-hot vector: all zeros, with a single 1 at position t. Multiply a one-hot vector by a matrix E and you get back row t of E, so in practice nobody multiplies; they just look the row up. That row is the token’s embedding. The trouble with one-hot vectors is that every pair of them is equally far apart: “king” is as unlike “queen” as it is unlike “cat”. A table of learned vectors can do better. Click a word, then compare one-hot, random and learned vectors.

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbf e_t &= E^{\top}\mathbf x_t = E_{t,:} \\ \mathbf x_t &= (0,\dots,0,\underset{t}{1},0,\dots,0) \\ E &\in \mathbb R^{|V|\times d} \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: xt is the one-hot vector for token t; multiplying by E picks out row t, a d-dimensional vector. The table has |V| × d numbers, all learned. In this chapter’s word vectors that is 6,000 × 100 = 600,000; in GPT-2 small it is 50,257 × 768 = 38,597,376, almost a third of the whole model.
Say it“The embedding of token t is E-transpose times the one-hot vector x-t, which is simply row t of E.”
token id
most similar of the other seven
average |cosine| between different words
numbers in the table

Where meaning comes from

You shall know a word by the company it keeps

Where should the learned numbers come from? The linguist J. R. Firth put the answer in one line in 1957, and Zellig Harris had said much the same in 1954: words that occur in similar contexts tend to mean similar things. You have never seen a wampimuk, but if it is fed, groomed and kept as a pet, you know roughly what it is. So count, for each word, how often every other word appears within a few positions of it. Raw counts are dominated by “the”, “of” and “and”, which keep company with everything. Pointwise mutual information asks a better question: does this pair occur together more often than chance? These are real counts from 17 million words of Wikipedia. Switch from counts to PPMI, widen the window, and click any cell.

\[ \begin{aligned} \text{PMI}(w,c) &= \log\frac{P(w,c)}{P(w)\,P(c)} \\ &= \log\frac{\#(w,c)\cdot D}{\#(w)\;\#(c)} \\ \text{PPMI}(w,c) &= \max\big(\text{PMI}(w,c),\ 0\big) \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: #(w,c) is how many times c fell within the window around w; #(w) and #(c) are each word’s total number of window partners; D is the total number of pairs; log is the natural log. If w and c were independent, P(w,c) would equal P(w)P(c) and PMI would be 0. Positive means “more often together than chance”. Negative values are noisy (they rest on tiny counts) and pairs never seen give −∞, so PPMI clips them to 0.
Say it“PMI of w and c is the log of their joint probability over the product of their separate probabilities; PPMI keeps only the positive part.”
#(w, c)
PMI
this row’s strongest context
pairs counted D

Compression

Squeezing the table with SVD

A row of the PPMI table is already a word vector, but a clumsy one: as long as the vocabulary, mostly zeros, and blind to the fact that “drink” and “wine” are related contexts. The singular value decomposition rewrites the table as a sum of rank-one layers, strongest first. Keep only the first k and you have the best possible rank-k approximation, and k numbers per word instead of thousands. Words that share contexts are forced to share coordinates. Below, the SVD of the 12 × 12 PPMI table from the last section is computed live. Lower the rank k and see how little the table loses, and where the words land.

\[ \begin{aligned} M &\approx M_k = U_k\,\Sigma_k\,V_k^{\top} \\ &= \sum_{i=1}^{k} \sigma_i\, \mathbf u_i \mathbf v_i^{\top} \\ \mathbf w_{\text{word}} &= \big(U_k\,\Sigma_k^{1/2}\big)_{\text{word},:} \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: M is the PPMI matrix; the σi are its singular values, largest first, and each term σiuivi⊤ is one layer. By the Eckart–Young theorem, no rank-k matrix is closer to M (in squared error) than Mk, and the error left over is the energy in the dropped σs. Each word’s vector is its row of UkΣk1/2 (taking the square root of Σ works better than Σ itself, Levy et al. 2015).
Say it“M is approximately U-k Sigma-k V-k transpose, the sum of the first k singular layers; a word’s vector is its row of U-k times the square root of Sigma-k.”
energy kept Σσ²
relative error ‖M − Mk‖ / ‖M‖
largest singular value σ₁
numbers per word

Meaning as geometry

Distances, directions and analogies

Do the same on the full 6,000 × 6,000 PPMI table of Wikipedia, keep k = 100, and every word becomes a point in 100 dimensions (the project shows how). Similarity is now an angle: the cosine of two vectors is 1 when they point the same way and near 0 when they are unrelated. Better still, some directions carry meaning. If the step from “france” to “paris” means “capital of”, then adding that same step to “germany” should land near “berlin”. This is the famous analogy test of Mikolov and colleagues (2013). It works more often than you would expect and fails more often than the headlines suggest. Pick an analogy, or click three words on the map to build your own.

\[ \cos(\mathbf a, \mathbf b) = \frac{\mathbf a^{\top}\mathbf b}{\Vert\mathbf a\Vert\,\Vert\mathbf b\Vert} \]
Read it as: the dot product of the two vectors divided by their lengths, so only the angle counts. Frequent words get longer vectors; dividing by length stops frequency from masquerading as meaning.
Say it“The cosine of a and b is their dot product over the product of their lengths.”
\[ d^\star = \arg\max_{d \,\notin\, \{a,b,c\}} \cos\big(\mathbf d,\ \mathbf b - \mathbf a + \mathbf c\big) \]
Read it as: “a is to b as c is to ?”: take b, remove a, add c, and return the word whose vector points most nearly that way, excluding the three question words (otherwise the answer is usually b or c itself).
Say it“d-star is the word, other than a, b and c, most aligned with b minus a plus c.”
answer d⋆
its cosine with b − a + c

Learning by prediction

word2vec: learn the vectors by guessing neighbours

Counting and factorising is one road. In 2013 Mikolov and colleagues took another: give every word two random vectors, one for when it is the centre word (v) and one for when it is a neighbour (u), and train them to tell real (word, neighbour) pairs from fake ones made by drawing random words. This is skip-gram with negative sampling, the heart of word2vec. Nothing in it mentions meaning, yet words that predict the same neighbours are pushed to the same place. Below, a tiny corpus of 400 sentences about animals, food and vehicles, and vectors with only 2 dimensions so you can watch them move. Press Train.

\[ \begin{aligned} \ell(w,c) &= -\log\sigma\big(\mathbf u_c^{\top}\mathbf v_w\big) \\ &\quad -\sum_{i=1}^{k}\log\sigma\big(-\mathbf u_{n_i}^{\top}\mathbf v_w\big) \\ n_i &\sim P(w)^{3/4} \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: σ is the logistic function, so σ(uc·vw) is the model’s probability that c really is a neighbour of w. The first term rewards a high score for the real pair; the sum punishes high scores for k random “negative” words ni, drawn in proportion to frequency to the power 3/4. Levy & Goldberg (2014) proved the link to the last sections: at its optimum, uc·vw = PMI(w, c) − log k. word2vec is secretly factorising a shifted PMI table.
Say it“The loss is minus log sigma of u-c dot v-w, minus the sum over k negatives of log sigma of minus u-n dot v-w.”
epochs
average loss per pair
distance within a group
distance across groups

One vector is not enough

Contextual embeddings

Every vector so far is static: “bank” gets one vector whether it holds money or water. In Wikipedia the money sense wins, so the static “bank” sits among monetary, fund and currency. To see which way a vector moves, we measure it against two anchor words that are not in the sentence, one for each sense. A contextual embedding is recomputed for every occurrence by mixing in the words around it. The machinery that does the mixing in every modern model is attention, and here is its simplest form: the word keeps its own vector and adds a weighted average of the other words’ vectors, weighting each by how similar it is. Nothing here is trained (real models learn what to compare and what to pass on, the subject of the next chapter), and only content words take part: “the”, “of” and friends are left out. Switch sentences, or type your own and click the word to contextualise.

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbf h_i &= \mathbf e_i + \lambda \sum_{j \ne i} \alpha_{ij}\,\mathbf e_j \\ \alpha_{ij} &= \frac{\exp\big(\cos(\mathbf e_i, \mathbf e_j)/\tau\big)}{\sum_{j' \ne i} \exp\big(\cos(\mathbf e_i, \mathbf e_{j'})/\tau\big)} \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: the new vector hi for word i is its static vector ei plus a blend of the other words’ static vectors. The weights αij are a softmax of similarities, so they are positive and sum to 1. The temperature τ sets how picky the blend is (small τ: listen mostly to the most similar word; large τ: listen to everyone equally), and λ how loudly the context speaks. Keeping ei and adding to it is the residual connection every transformer layer uses.
Say it“h-i is e-i plus lambda times the sum over the other words of alpha-i-j times e-j, where alpha is a softmax of cosines divided by tau.”
Nearest words to the contextual vector

Real-world project

Project: a tokeniser for Austen, a word map of Wikipedia

Two real artefacts, built the way the first generation of neural language models built theirs. First, a byte-pair tokeniser trained, merge by merge, in your browser on chapters 1–50 of Pride and Prejudice (Project Gutenberg eBook #1342) and tested on chapters 51–61. Second, word vectors for the 6,000 commonest words of text8, Matt Mahoney’s cleaned first 100 million characters of a 2006 English Wikipedia dump (17,005,207 lowercase words, numbers spelt out). Those were built offline in numpy and scipy exactly as in the sections above: PPMI over a 5-word window, with context counts raised to the power 0.75 as Levy, Goldberg & Dagan (2015) recommend, then a rank-100 SVD. The page carries the result in 8 bits per number and recomputes everything else live.

Two standard tests. WordSim-353 (Finkelstein et al., 2002): people rated how related 353 word pairs are, from 0 to 10; 213 pairs have both words in our vocabulary, and we measure the Spearman rank correlation between their ratings and our cosines. The Google analogy set (Mikolov et al., 2013): 19,544 questions such as athens : greece :: baghdad : ?, of which 3,084 use only our 6,000 words; a question counts only if the single best answer, searched over all 6,000 words, is exactly right.

The same project in Python

import re, collections, numpy as np, scipy.sparse as sp
from scipy.sparse.linalg import svds
from scipy.stats import spearmanr

# ---------- 1. BPE on Pride and Prejudice: train on chapters 1-50, test on 51-61 ----------
raw = open("pg1342.txt", encoding="utf-8").read()
t = raw[raw.index("Chapter I.]") + 11: raw.index("[Illustration:\n\n                                  THE")]
t = re.sub(r"\[Illustration[^\]]*\]", " ", t).replace("_", "")
chapters = re.split(r"\n\s*(?:CHAPTER|Chapter) [IVXLC]+\.?\s*\n", t); assert len(chapters) == 61
pre = lambda s: re.findall(r"[A-Za-z]+|[0-9]+|[^\sA-Za-z0-9]", s)   # words, numbers, single symbols
train = collections.Counter(w for ch in chapters[:50] for w in pre(ch))
test = collections.Counter(w for ch in chapters[50:] for w in pre(ch))

def merge(sy, a, b):
    out, i = [], 0
    while i < len(sy):
        if i + 1 < len(sy) and sy[i] == a and sy[i + 1] == b: out.append(a + b); i += 2
        else: out.append(sy[i]); i += 1
    return out

def bpe_train(freq, n_merges):
    words = {w: list(w) + ["_"] for w in freq}                    # "_" marks the end of a word
    merges = []
    for _ in range(n_merges):
        pairs = collections.Counter()
        for w, sy in words.items():
            for a, b in zip(sy, sy[1:]): pairs[a, b] += freq[w]
        (a, b), n = min(pairs.items(), key=lambda kv: (-kv[1], kv[0]))  # most frequent; ties: alphabetical
        merges.append((a, b, n))
        for w, sy in words.items():
            if a in sy: words[w] = merge(sy, a, b)
    return merges

def tokens_per_word(freq, merges):
    segs = {w: list(w) + ["_"] for w in freq}
    out = {0: sum(len(s) * freq[w] for w, s in segs.items()) / sum(freq.values())}
    for m, (a, b, _) in enumerate(merges, 1):
        for w, sy in segs.items():
            if a in sy: segs[w] = merge(sy, a, b)
        if m in (100, 500, 1000, 2000, 3000): out[m] = sum(len(s) * freq[w] for w, s in segs.items()) / sum(freq.values())
    return out, segs

merges = bpe_train(train, 3000)
alphabet = sorted({ch for w in train for ch in w} | {"_"})
print(f"BPE: {len(chapters)} chapters, {sum(train.values())} training words ({len(train)} types), alphabet {len(alphabet)}")
print("first 10 merges:", " ".join(f"{a}+{b}({n})" for a, b, n in merges[:10]))
print("merges 2991-3000:", " ".join(a + b for a, b, _ in merges[-10:]))
tpw, segs = tokens_per_word(test, merges)
print("held-out tokens per word:", {m: round(v, 4) for m, v in tpw.items()})
unseen = sorted((w for w in test if w not in train), key=lambda w: (-test[w], w))
print(f"{len(unseen)} held-out word types never seen in training; the commonest, after 3000 merges:", " ".join("|".join(segs[w]) for w in unseen[:6]))

# ---------- 2. word vectors: PPMI + SVD on text8 (17 million words of Wikipedia) ----------
words = open("text8").read().split()
V, L, K = 6000, 5, 100
cnt = collections.Counter(words)
vocab = [w for w, _ in sorted(cnt.items(), key=lambda x: (-x[1], x[0]))[:V]]
ix = {w: i for i, w in enumerate(vocab)}
ids = np.fromiter((ix.get(w, -1) for w in words), dtype=np.int32, count=len(words))
C = sp.csr_matrix((V, V))
for d in range(1, L + 1):                                         # symmetric window of 5 words
    a, b = ids[:-d], ids[d:]; m = (a >= 0) & (b >= 0)
    C = C + sp.coo_matrix((np.ones(m.sum()), (a[m], b[m])), shape=(V, V)).tocsr()
C = (C + C.T).tocoo()
D = C.sum(); pw = np.bincount(C.row, C.data, V) / D
pc = np.bincount(C.col, C.data, V) ** 0.75; pc /= pc.sum()        # context-distribution smoothing
pmi = np.log(C.data / D / (pw[C.row] * pc[C.col])); keep = pmi > 0
M = sp.csr_matrix((pmi[keep], (C.row[keep], C.col[keep])), shape=(V, V))
U, s, _ = svds(M, k=K, v0=np.random.default_rng(0).standard_normal(V))
o = np.argsort(-s); U, s = U[:, o], s[o]
print(f"\ntext8: {len(words)} words, vocabulary {V}, {int(D)} co-occurrences, PPMI nonzeros {keep.sum()}")
print("top singular values:", np.round(s[:5], 2))

def vectors(k): W = U[:, :k] * np.sqrt(s[:k]); return W / np.linalg.norm(W, axis=1, keepdims=True)
def nearest(W, w, n=6): sim = W @ W[ix[w]]; return [(vocab[i], round(float(sim[i]), 3)) for i in np.argsort(-sim)[1:n + 1]]
def analogy(W, a, b, c):                                          # a : b :: c : ?   (3CosAdd)
    sim = W @ (W[ix[b]] - W[ix[a]] + W[ix[c]])
    sim[[ix[a], ix[b], ix[c]]] = -np.inf
    return vocab[int(sim.argmax())]

ws = [(a, b, float(x)) for a, b, x in (l.split("\t") for l in open("ws353.txt").read().split("\n") if l) if a in ix and b in ix]
qs = [l.lower().split() for l in open("questions-words.txt") if not l.startswith(":")]
qs = np.array([[ix[w] for w in q] for q in qs if all(w in ix for w in q)])
for k in (2, 10, 25, 50, 100):
    W = vectors(k)
    rho = spearmanr([W[ix[a]] @ W[ix[b]] for a, b, _ in ws], [x for *_, x in ws]).statistic
    sim = (W[qs[:, 1]] - W[qs[:, 0]] + W[qs[:, 2]]) @ W.T
    for j in range(3): sim[np.arange(len(qs)), qs[:, j]] = -np.inf
    acc = (sim.argmax(1) == qs[:, 3]).mean()
    print(f"k = {k:3d}: WordSim-353 Spearman {rho:.3f} on {len(ws)} pairs, analogy accuracy {acc:.3f} on {len(qs)} questions")
W = vectors(100)
for w in ("king", "bank", "france", "computer"): print(w, "->", nearest(W, w))
for q in (("france", "paris", "germany"), ("brother", "sister", "son"), ("man", "king", "woman")): print(" : ".join(q), ": ?  ->", analogy(W, *q))

The browser’s BPE is an independent JavaScript implementation (incremental pair counts rather than recounting); it reproduces Python’s 3,000 merges in the same order, with the same counts, and the same held-out tokens per word to four decimals. The word vectors differ from Python’s only by the 8-bit rounding the page needs to stay small: at k = 100 that moves Spearman’s ρ from 0.7003 to 0.7004 and the analogy score from 1,248 to 1,246 correct; the table above compares the browser with Python run on the same 8-bit vectors, which it matches. Two honest caveats. text8 is small by modern standards (the published word2vec vectors were trained on about 100 billion words of Google News), so 40% on analogies is respectable for PPMI–SVD at this scale but well short of the 60–65% Mikolov and colleagues reported with a billion words or more. And the t-SNE map in the hero (van der Maaten & Hinton, 2008) was computed offline with scikit-learn; its distances are only roughly faithful, which is why the neighbours it highlights are always computed in the full 100 dimensions.

Wrap-up

Five lines to remember

  • A tokeniser turns text into integers from a fixed vocabulary; characters make sequences long, whole words leave unknowns, subwords sit in between.
  • BPE learns its vocabulary by repeatedly gluing the most frequent neighbouring pair; the ordered merge list is the tokeniser, and the number of merges trades vocabulary size for sequence length.
  • An embedding is a row of a learned table, looked up by token id; it is the same as multiplying a one-hot vector by the table.
  • Meaning comes from company: PPMI counts which words co-occur more than chance, and a truncated SVD (or word2vec, which implicitly factorises shifted PMI) turns that into short dense vectors.
  • In those vectors similarity is an angle and some relations are directions, but static vectors give one point per word; contextual embeddings, built by attention, give one per occurrence.

Check your understanding

Why can a byte-level BPE tokeniser (like GPT-2’s) never produce an unknown token?

Its starting alphabet is all 256 byte values, and any text, in any language or script, is a sequence of bytes. Merges only ever glue existing symbols, so every input can always fall back to single bytes.

You double the number of BPE merges. What happens to the vocabulary, to sequence length, and to the size of the embedding table?

The vocabulary grows by exactly the number of new merges; sequences get shorter, but with diminishing returns (each new merge is rarer than the last); and the embedding table (and the output layer) grows in proportion to |V|, so each rare token gets fewer training examples.

Two different words have one-hot vectors with cosine 0. What is the cosine of two random 100-dimensional Gaussian vectors, roughly, and why?

Close to 0, typically within about ±0.1 (the spread is about 1/√100): in high dimensions random directions are nearly perpendicular. Neither one-hot nor random vectors carry similarity; only learning puts related words at small angles.

Why does PMI favour rare context words, and what does the 0.75 power on context counts do about it?

A rare context that happens to co-occur a few times gets a huge ratio P(w,c)/(P(w)P(c)), because P(c) is tiny. Raising context counts to 0.75 inflates small probabilities a little, which shrinks those ratios and tames the bias (Levy, Goldberg & Dagan 2015).

In this chapter king − man + woman gives “prince”, not “queen”. Does that mean the vectors are broken?

No. In Wikipedia “king” is surrounded by regnal numbers and royal vocabulary, so its vector is dominated by “royalty”, and the gender offset is small by comparison. Analogy arithmetic works when the relation is a large, consistent direction (capitals, plurals, tenses) and is fragile otherwise; queen still ranks in the top 15 of 6,000.
